title: The contact engine inside a simulation

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Imagine a simulation where two surfaces slide against each other, and the program has to know exactly when they touch and how much they resist. Someone has to do that math. In many projects, it's IPC Toolkit.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Not a full one. It's a C plus plus library focused only on contact. Your application keeps the time-stepping loop and the solver, and calls the library whenever it needs contact answers.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Like a specialist you phone for one hard question.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's a good picture. The simulation passes in collision geometry and how the vertices move. The library first picks candidate pairs in a broad phase, then checks them precisely with continuous collision detection, and hands the result back.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Four families. Collision detection, in broad and narrow phases. Distance derivatives for edges and triangles. Contact barriers, meaning functions that keep surfaces from passing through each other, including adaptive stiffness. And friction potentials, smooth or lagged.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And what's Antoine's part in it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He contributes to it as open source. His fork is where he stages changes before proposing them to the upstream project. One merged contribution adds anisotropic friction, where grip depends on direction. Another merged one lets you pass parameters to the Scalable CCD narrow phase.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He also drafted adhesion documentation that was merged, and fixed a Windows CUDA build issue in the Scalable CCD project, the GPU collision detection path.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. Friction that depends on direction and material pair, which is exactly what his thesis work on surface wear needed from the contact model. Plus the GPU collision path, which the Windows build and parameter pass-through opened up.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the library and his research feed each other.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. If you want to see complete simulations using it, the upstream project points to PolyFEM and Rigid IPC. The full write-up has the architecture diagram and the list of pull requests.
